results.authors: Thomalla G, Simonsen CZ, Boutitie F, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with unknown time of onset and an acute DWI lesion without marked FLAIR hyperintensity (DWI-FLAIR mismatch), IV alteplase improved 90-day functional outcome compared with placebo.
results.title: MRI-guided thrombolysis for stroke with unknown time of onset (WAKE-UP)

results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, Parsons MW, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients 4.5 to 9 hours from onset, or with wake-up stroke within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep, who had salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging (core under 70 mL, mismatch ratio above 1.2, mismatch volume above 10 mL) and no planned thrombectomy, IV alteplase increased excellent functional outcome at 90 days, with more symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage.
results.title: Thrombolysis guided by perfusion imaging up to 9 hours after onset of stroke (EXTEND)

results.authors: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al.
results.key_finding: For wake-up or unknown-onset stroke, IV thrombolysis is reasonable either with a DWI-positive, FLAIR-negative lesion, or within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep with salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging in patients not eligible for thrombectomy.
results.title: 2026 AHA/ASA guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke

output.summary: Two imaging pathways select wake-up or unknown-onset stroke patients for IV thrombolysis: a DWI-FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP), and, within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep in patients not eligible for thrombectomy, penumbral mismatch on automated perfusion imaging (EXTEND criteria: core under 70 mL, ratio above 1.2, mismatch above 10 mL). The 1.8 ratio with mismatch above 15 mL comes from thrombectomy-selection and tenecteplase trials (DEFUSE 3, TIMELESS), not from EXTEND.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for the paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 5; HAS-BLED 4 once aspirin is stopped; only one dose-reduction criterion, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, so no reduction) on day 6 to 7 once follow-up imaging excludes hemorrhagic transformation, since the infarct (about 18 mL, posterior frontal and parietal cortex) spans more than one cortical branch of the superior division, the ELAN major category; stop aspirin and do not bridge with heparin.

Refer the symptomatic 55-60% left ICA stenosis, ipsilateral to the infarct, for vascular surgical review within 2 weeks: the AF burden makes cardioembolism the leading mechanism, but the stenosis is a competing one, and endarterectomy for a symptomatic 50-69% stenosis is decided on patient factors (older men benefit most) when perioperative risk is below 6% (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention); if surgery is not chosen, continue anticoagulation with intensive lipid lowering and risk-factor control.
Intensify lipid lowering for the carotid and intracranial atherosclerosis (LDL 126 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg): add ezetimibe 10 mg and escalate further if LDL stays at or above 70 mg/dL.
Treat hyperglycemia (glucose 237 mg/dL) to 140-180 mg/dL during the first 24 hours, avoiding hypoglycemia, and intensify diabetes treatment (HbA1c 9.0%).

Investigate the microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, MCV 78 fL) with iron studies and, if iron deficient, a gastrointestinal evaluation; it raises bleeding risk on anticoagulation but does not by itself contraindicate it.

Treat the other vascular risk factors: smoking cessation, CPAP adherence for obstructive sleep apnea, and resumption of amlodipine and losartan after the first 48 to 72 hours with a long-term blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg.

clinical_pearls: The WAKE-UP trial established DWI-FLAIR mismatch as a tissue clock for wake-up strokes: DWI+/FLAIR- suggests onset within 4.5 hours and eligibility for thrombolysis; DWI+/FLAIR+ closes only this limb, and perfusion imaging by EXTEND criteria can still qualify a patient not eligible for thrombectomy within 9 hours of the sleep midpoint
Up to 25% of cryptogenic strokes in patients over 55 are attributed to paroxysmal AF detected on prolonged monitoring; a single ECG is insufficient to exclude this diagnosis
Left atrial enlargement on ECG or echocardiography is a strong predictor of underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and should lower the threshold for prolonged cardiac monitoring
Hemineglect with a dominant (left) hemisphere lesion is less common and typically more subtle than with non-dominant (right) hemisphere strokes, making it easier to miss on routine examination

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Michael Patterson is a 73-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease who presents to the emergency department after waking at approximately 06:45 this morning with new-onset slurred speech and difficulty using his right hand. He reports going to bed at approximately 23:00 the previous evening feeling entirely at his baseline. He woke once around 03:00 to use the bathroom and does not recall any difficulty at that time, though he acknowledges he was groggy and did not pay close attention to his coordination or speech. When his alarm went off at 06:45, he noticed his speech sounded thick and he had trouble gripping his phone. He also felt mildly unsteady when walking to the bathroom. He initially attributed these symptoms to having slept in an awkward position and waited approximately 45 minutes to see if they would resolve. When the symptoms persisted, his daughter called him at 07:30 during her morning routine, noticed his slurred speech over the phone, and urged him to call 911. EMS arrived at 07:52 and identified right facial droop and mild right arm weakness. A prehospital stroke alert was activated with a Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale score of 2. His fingerstick glucose in the field was 204 mg/dL. He arrived at the ED at 08:14. On initial assessment, the patient reports a mild headache over the left temporal region but denies any visual changes, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, or seizure-like activity. He cannot say for certain whether the symptoms were present when he woke at 03:00, making the last known well time approximately 23:00 the previous evening, roughly 9 hours prior to ED arrival. He has no history of prior stroke or TIA. He ran out of his amlodipine approximately one week ago and has not refilled it.
